ai_summary: Great Britain's wind output currently reaches 5.4 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output contributing 2.6 GW, representing 25.7% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Thanks to this abundant renewable generation, Scottish carbon intensity has dropped to 0 gCO2/kWh, compared to a GB-wide figure of 199 gCO2/kWh. However, persistent cross-border transmission constraints prevent this zero-carbon electricity from flowing south to major demand centres. Consequently, 83.5 GWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed so far today through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring a direct constraint cost of about £2,836,356. To replace this blocked clean power, thermal plants elsewhere on the network were forced to ramp up, burning an estimated 15,868,572 m3 of gas and emitting 29,232 tonnes CO2 into the atmosphere. Extrapolated across a full year, this run-rate suggests an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of £1,035 million. Because balancing and constraint payments are socialised across all electricity consumers, an annualised constraint overhead on this scale increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £4/MWh. This dual financial and environmental penalty clearly underscores the pressing need to expand transmission capacity between Scotland and England.
